Alif-Lam-Mim. If it is taken as the name of the surah, it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is "The revelation of the Book" (tanzil al-kitab). If it is taken as an enumeration of the letters, then "The revelation of the Book" is raised as the predicate of an omitted subject. Or it is a subject whose predicate is "there is no doubt in it" (la rayba fihi). The better view is that "the revelation of the Book" is raised as a subject, and its predicate is "from the Lord of the worlds" (min rabb al-alamin). "There is no doubt in it" is then a parenthetical clause (i'tiraD) with no grammatical place in the sentence. The pronoun in "fihi" refers to the content of the whole clause, as if it were said: "there is no doubt in that", that is, in its being sent down from the Lord of the worlds. The soundness of this view is confirmed by His saying: "Or do they say, 'He has invented it'?" For their saying "this is invented" is a denial that it could be from the Lord of the worlds. Likewise His saying: "Rather, it is the truth from your Lord" (al-haqq min rabbika), and what it implies of the assumption that it is from Allah. This is a sound and firm method: He first affirmed that its revelation is from the Lord of the worlds, and that this is beyond doubt; then He turned away from that to His saying "Or do they say, 'He has invented it'?", because "am" here is the disjunctive "am" which carries the meaning of "bal" (rather) together with the interrogative hamza, denying their claim and expressing wonder at it, given the evident nature of its matter, namely the inability of their eloquent men to produce anything like three verses of it. Then He turned from the denial to affirming that it is the truth from your Lord. A parallel to this is when a scholar in a question gives a correct, comprehensive reason, in which he has guarded against every kind of objection, as the theologians' saying: "Reflection (al-nazar) is the first of the obligatory acts absolutely, from which no responsible person is free." Then an objection is raised against him concerning some matter he had guarded against, and he answers it by explaining that he had already guarded against that, and then returns to establishing his statement and carrying it through.

If you say: how can He negate that there is doubt that it is from Allah, when He has affirmed something graver than doubt, namely their saying "He has invented it"? I say: the meaning of "there is no doubt in it" is that doubt has no entry into its being the revelation of Allah, because what removes doubt and clears it away is inseparable from it, namely its being inimitable to humans, and that is farthest of all things from doubt. As for their saying "He has invented it", it is either the saying of one who is obstinate while knowing that it is from Allah, because the miraculous nature is evident to him, or of an ignorant person who says it before reflection and consideration, because he heard people saying it.

"Such that there had not come to them any warner before you" (ma atahum min nadhirin min qablika), like His saying: "as their fathers were not warned" (ma undhira aba'uhum). That is because Allah had not sent a messenger to Quraysh before him (ﷺ).

[Mahmud said: "I mean Quraysh, because no prophet was ever sent to them. If you say: if no prophet was sent to them before, then the proof was not established against them in matters. I say: the establishment of proof by the laws which can only be known through messengers has no way to be. As for its establishment by knowledge of Allah the Exalted, His unity and His wisdom, yes, because the proofs of reason are with them in every age." Ahmad said: The position of the people of the Sunnah is that the knowledge of none of the legal rulings of Allah the Exalted is attained except through the revealed law. What al-Zamakhshari mentioned is a derivation from the principle of the goodness and ugliness of things by reason, which the revealed texts have rejected, so the pen does not permit it; he turned away from it until he plunged into talk about something else. The proof was established upon the Arabs through the messengers who came before them, such as their forefather Isma'il and others. The intended meaning of His saying "any warner had not come to them" is the descendants of the Arabs in the time of him (ﷺ), since no contemporary warner had been sent to them, so Allah in His kindness to them sent among them a messenger from themselves.]

"So that they may be guided" (la'allahum yahtadun): in this there are two possibilities. Either it is an expression of hope (tarajji) from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as in "perhaps he may remember" (la'allahu yatadhakkaru), an expression of hope from Musa and Harun (peace be upon them); or the word of hope is used metaphorically for intention (irada).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 32, verse 4:

If you ask: what is the meaning of His words ﴿You have no protector or intercessor besides Him﴾? I answer: it has two meanings. The first is that if you turn away from His good pleasure, you will find for yourselves no protector (waliyy), that is, no helper who will help you, nor any intercessor (shafi') who will intercede for you. The second is that Allah is your protector (waliyy), who manages your affairs, and your intercessor (shafi'), that is, your helper, in a figurative sense (majaz), because the intercessor supports the one for whom he intercedes. This is like His words, exalted is He: ﴿And you have no protector or helper besides Allah﴾. So when He forsakes you, there remains for you no protector and no helper.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 32, verse 5:

The command (al-amr al-ma'mur bihi) of acts of obedience and righteous deeds, He sends it down, arranged (mudabbiran), from the heaven to the earth; then it is not acted upon, nor does it ascend to Him, that commanded thing pure as He wills and approves, except after a long duration, due to the scarcity of God's workers and His sincere servants, and the scarcity of ascending deeds, because ascension (ṣu'ūd) is only attributed to what is pure (al-khāliṣ). This is indicated by His saying following it: ﴿little is it that you give thanks﴾. Or: He arranges the affair of the whole world from the heaven to the earth, for each day of God's days, which is a thousand years, as He said: ﴿And indeed a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾. Then it ascends to Him (thumma ya'ruju ilayhi), meaning it reaches Him and remains with Him, and He records in the scrolls of His angels, at every moment of these durations, what rises of that affair and enters into existence, until the duration reaches its end. Then He arranges again for another day, and so on until the Hour is established. It was also said: the revelation descends with Jibril, peace be upon him, from the heaven to the earth, then there returns to Him what was of the acceptance of the revelation or its rejection, with Jibril, and that happens in a time which is in reality a thousand years, because the distance is a journey of a thousand years in descent and ascent, since the distance between the heaven and the earth is a journey of five hundred years, and it is one of your days because of the speed of Jibril, for he covers a journey of a thousand years in one day. It was also said: He arranges the affair of the world from the heaven to the earth until the Hour is established, then that entire affair ascends to Him, meaning it reaches Him to judge concerning it, in a Day whose measure is a thousand years, and it is the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Abi 'Ablah read: ya'ruju, in the passive form (al-bina' lil-maf'ul). And it was read: ya'udduna, with the ta' and with the ya'.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 32, verses 6–9:

ﺃَﺣْﺴَﻦَ ﻛُﻞَّ ﺷَﻲْﺀٍ ﺣَﺴَّﻨﻪ ("He made excellent everything He created"): that is, He made everything good, because there is nothing He created that is not arranged according to what wisdom requires and what benefit necessitates. All created things are therefore good, though they differ in degrees of goodness, some good and some better, as He said: ﴿Indeed, We created man in the best of stature﴾. It has also been said that the meaning is: He taught how to create it, from the saying "a person's worth is what he does well" (qimat al-mar' ma yuhsin). Its real sense is: He knows it well, that is, He knows it with a good knowledge, with precision and mastery.

It is read as khalaqahu (a substitution, badal), meaning: He made excellent, so He created everything. [[The phrase "fa-qad khalaqa" ("so He created") is perhaps an addition by the copyist. The wording of al-Nasafi is: "as a substitution, meaning: He made excellent the creation of everything." It is possible that it is not an addition, but rather this is the meaning arrived at through the substitution reading, just as its reverse, mentioned later, is the meaning arrived at through the attributive reading. (ʿ)]] And it is read as khalaqahu (as an attribute, wasf), meaning: everything He created, He made excellent.

The offspring is called nasl because it issues forth from him, that is, it separates from him and comes out of his loins. Similar to this is their saying of a child: salil and najl. [[The phrase "and it comes out of his loins" suggests a lost passage before it, whose sense would be: just as the drop of semen is called sulala because it is drawn from him. In the Sihah, "al-najl" means offspring, and "najlahu" means his father, that is, his child. (ʿ)]]

ﻭَﺳَﻮَّﺍﻩُ ("and He shaped him"): He straightened him, like His saying ﴿in the best of stature﴾.

By attributing the spirit to His own self, He indicates that it is a wondrous creation whose reality none knows but Him, like His saying ﴿And they ask you about the spirit...﴾ (the verse). It is as if He said: and He breathed into him from that thing which He alone has and which only He knows.

And they say: "When we have gone astray in the earth, shall we indeed be [raised] in a new creation?" The speaker was Ubayy ibn Khalaf, but since they all agreed with his words, the statement is attributed to them all. It is also read: ﴿أَئِنَّا﴾ (a-innā), and ﴿وَأَنَّا﴾ (wa-annā), with the interrogative omitted.

ضَلَلْنا (ḍalalnā) means: we became dust, and we went and mixed with the earth's dust, such that we are not distinguished from it, as water gets lost in milk. Or: "we were hidden in the earth" by burial in it, from the verse of the poet:

وَآبَ مُضَلُّوهُ بِعَيْنٍ جَلِيَّةٍ ... وَغُودِرَ بِالجَوْلانِ حَزْمٌ وَنائِلُ

[The one who buried him returned with a clear eye (i.e., with open, unconcealed grief), and there was left at al-Jawlan (a mountain in Syria) the firmness and the generosity (of the dead man). He is lamenting a dead man. al-iyab (إياب) means return; al-idlal (الإضلال) means burial and concealment; al-Jawlan is a mountain in Syria; al-nā'il means giving. The meaning: by leaving that person, who was described by firmness and generosity, those qualities were left there.]

It is read by ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both) as ﴿ضَلِلْنا﴾ (ḍaliltnā) with a kasra on the lām. It is said: ḍalla yaḍillu and ḍalla yaḍallu. Al-Ḥasan (may Allah be pleased with him) read it as ﴿صَلَلْنا﴾ (ṣalalnā), from ṣalla al-laḥm and aṣalla, meaning: when the meat became putrid. It is also said: "we became of the substance of ṣalla," which is the earth.

If you ask: by what is the adverbial ﴿إِذا ضَلَلْنا﴾ governed? I say: by what is implied by ﴿إِنَّا لَفِي خَلْقٍ جَدِيدٍ﴾, namely "we will be resurrected," or "He will renew our creation."

﴿لِقاءِ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ (liqāʾi rabbihim, the meeting with their Lord): this is reaching the outcome, from receiving the Angel of Death and what lies beyond him. When He mentioned their denial of the (first) creation, He turned from it to what is more emphatic in disbelief, which is that they deny everything that will occur in the outcome, not the (first) creation alone. Do you not see how they were addressed with the taking of their souls by the Angel of Death, and with returning to their Lord afterwards, raised for reckoning and recompense? This is the meaning of "meeting Allah," as we have mentioned.

﴿التَّوَفِّي﴾ (al-tawaffī, the taking up) is the complete taking of the soul, which is the spirit. It is also said: the Angel of Death calls the spirits and they respond to him, then he commands his helpers to seize them.

And they say: "When we have gone astray in the earth, shall we indeed be [raised] in a new creation?" The speaker was Ubayy ibn Khalaf, but since they all agreed with his words, the statement is attributed to them all. It is also read: ﴿أَئِنَّا﴾ (a-innā), and ﴿وَأَنَّا﴾ (wa-annā), with the interrogative omitted.

[The one who buried him returned with a clear eye (i.e., with open, unconcealed grief), and there was left at al-Jawlan (a mountain in Syria) the firmness and the generosity (of the dead man). He is lamenting a dead man. al-iyab (إياب) means return; al-idlal (الإضلال) means burial and concealment; al-Jawlan is a mountain in Syria; al-nā'il means giving. The meaning: by leaving that person, who was described by firmness and generosity, those qualities were left there.]

It is also said: "we became of the substance of ṣalla," which is the earth.

When He mentioned their denial of the (first) creation, He turned from it to what is more emphatic in disbelief, which is that they deny everything that will occur in the outcome, not the (first) creation alone. Do you not see how they were addressed with the taking of their souls by the Angel of Death, and with returning to their Lord afterwards, raised for reckoning and recompense? This is the meaning of "meeting Allah," as we have mentioned.

And if only you could see (wa law tara) may be addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and it has two meanings. The first is that it expresses a wish (tamanni), as if he had said: "I wish you could see," like the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying to al-Mughira: "If only you had looked at her." [This is part of a hadith related by al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, Ahmad, al-Bazzar and others, from al-Mughira, that he proposed to a woman, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him, "Look at her, for that is more likely to create affection between you." Abu 'Ubayd related it in al-Gharib with the wording that he said to al-Mughira, when he had proposed to a woman, "If only you had looked at her," and the hadith continues.] A wish is possible for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), just as hope (taraji) was possible for him in ﴿that perhaps they may be guided﴾, because he swallowed their grief and bore their enmity and harm. So Allah granted him a wish to see them in that dreadful state of shame, humiliation and sorrow, so that he might gloat over them. The particle law here is the conditional "if," whose answer has been omitted, and the answer is: "you would have seen a dreadful matter," or "you would have seen the worst state." It is also permissible that it is addressed to everyone, as when you say: "So-and-so is base; if you honour him, he humiliates you, and if you do good to him, he harms you." You do not mean a particular addressee, so it is as if you had said: "If he is honoured, and if he is done good to..."

Both law and idha are for the past tense. That is permissible because what is awaited from Allah is as though it already existed and was certain to occur. Ra'a (see) does not need an object specified; it is as if it were said: "If there were to be seeing on your part," and idha (when) is an adverbial clause related to it.

They cry for help with their words ﴿Our Lord, we have seen and we have heard﴾, so they are not helped. The meaning is: we have seen the truth of Your promise and Your threat, and we have heard from You the confirmation of Your messengers. Or: we were blind and deaf, and then we saw and heard. ﴿So return us﴾, which means return to the world. ﴿We would have given every soul its guidance﴾ by way of compulsion and coercion, but We built the matter on choice rather than necessity. [The statement "but We built the matter on choice" is this: when the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school) made it obligatory for Allah to do what is best (al-salah), they said: He willed guidance for all, but with a will of choice (mashi'at takhyir), not a will of compulsion (mashi'at ijbar). That is why not all were guided, only some. Had He willed with a will of coercion, all would have been guided.

The Ahl al-Sunna (the people of the Sunna) did not make anything obligatory upon Allah. They said: whatever Allah wills occurs, and whatever He does not will does not occur, whether it is good or evil. The fact that will entails the occurrence of what is willed does not entail coercion or compulsion of the servants, because they have acquisition (kasb) in their actions, even though those actions are in reality created by Allah, as is established in the science of tawhid. (ʿ)] Not by necessity, so they preferred blindness over guidance, and the word of punishment was justified against the people of blindness, not the seeing. Do you not see what He followed it with: ﴿So taste [it] for what you forgot﴾? He made tasting the punishment a result of their deed: forgetting the outcome, little thought about it, and neglecting to prepare for it. Nisyan (forgetting) here means the opposite of remembrance. The meaning is that immersion in desires distracted you and diverted you from remembering the outcome, and forgetting it took hold of you. Then He said ﴿Indeed We have forgotten you﴾ by way of correspondence, that is: We recompense you with a recompense for your forgetting. It has also been said that it means abandonment: you abandoned reflection on the outcome, so We abandon you from mercy. The beginning of the sentence ﴿Indeed We have forgotten you﴾ with the construction of the verb on inna and its noun is an intensification in punishing them. The meaning is: taste this, that is, what you are in of lowered heads, shame and sorrow because of forgetting the meeting, and taste the everlasting punishment in Hell because of what you did, ﴿of sins and grave transgressions﴾. Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: It has been established among the positions of the Ahl al-Sunna that what necessitates deserving everlasting punishment is disbelief alone. As for lesser major sins, they do not require eternity. The question is one transmitted by revelation, and its evidences from the Qur'an and Sunna are definitive, in opposition to the Qadariyya (the school that denied divine predestination).] "Grave destructive sins" means those that destroy, i.e. that bring ruin. (ʿ)

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 32, verse 15–17:

﴿Those who, when they are reminded of them,﴾ that is, are admonished, fall down in prostration, humbling themselves before God and in awe, and giving thanks for what He has provided them of Islam, ﴿and glorify the praise of their Lord,﴾ that is, they declare God free of attributing ugliness to Him, and they praise Him, extolling Him, ﴿and they are not arrogant.﴾ Unlike one who persists in arrogance as if he had not heard them. A similar verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it, when it is recited to them, fall down on their faces in prostration, and say: "Glory be to our Lord"﴾. ﴿They forsake their beds﴾: they rise up and withdraw from ﴿the beds﴾, from the couches and places of sleep, calling upon their Lord and worshipping Him, out of fear of His wrath and hope for His mercy. They are the ones who pray at night (al-mutahajjidun). It is narrated from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) concerning its interpretation: "The standing of a servant at night" [[Narrated by Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ishaq and al-Hakim, from the narration of Abu Wa'il from Mu'adh in the course of a marfu' hadith, in which he said: "And a man's prayer in the depths of the night," then he recited: "Their sides forsake their beds."]]. And from al-Hasan, may God be pleased with him, that it is the tahajjud (night prayer). And from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "When God gathers the first and the last on the Day of Resurrection, a herald will call out with a voice that all creatures hear: 'The people of the gathering will know today who is worthier of honour.' Then he returns and calls: 'Let those stand whose sides forsook their beds,' and they stand, and they are few. Then he returns and calls: 'Let those stand who used to praise God in adversity and hardship,' and they stand, and they are few, and they all go forth together into Paradise. Then the rest of the people are judged." [[Narrated by Ishaq and Abu Ya'la, from the narration of Shahr ibn Hawshab from Asma' bint Yazid at length, and it is in al-Hakim in summary.]]. And from Anas ibn Malik, may God be pleased with him: some of the companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to pray between the Maghrib prayer and the late 'Isha' prayer, and this verse was revealed concerning them. [[Narrated by Ibn Mardawayh from the narration of al-Harith ibn Rahbah from Malik ibn Dinar: "I asked Anas ibn Malik about His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾ — the verse," and he said: "Some people—" and he mentioned it. Abu Dawud related a similar report from a hadith of Sa'id from Qatadah from Anas. He said: al-Hasan used to say, "It is the standing in the night." And al-Bazzar (narrated) by way of Zayd ibn Aslam from his father. He said: Bilal said, "We used to sit while some of the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed after Maghrib until 'Isha,' and then this verse was revealed." He said: We do not know of any chain for it except this one, and Aslam did not narrate from Bilal except him.]] It is also said: they are those who perform the 'atamah prayer and do not sleep through it. ﴿What is hidden for them﴾ is read in the passive form (ukhfiya). ﴿What He has hidden for them﴾ with the verb in the active, its subject being God, glorified is He. ﴿What We have hidden for them﴾ and ﴿What I have hidden for them﴾: these three forms are first person, and the speaker is God, glorified is He. ﴿What﴾ means "that which," or it means "what" (ayy shay'). [[His saying "or it means ayy" is perhaps: "ayy shay'" (what thing) (ʿ)]]. It is also read: ﴿qurrati a'yunin﴾ (coolness of eyes) and ﴿qurrata a'yunin﴾. The meaning: no soul knows—none of them, neither a nearest angel nor a sent prophet—what immense kind of reward God has stored up for those and hidden from all His creatures, which none knows but Him, of that which will delight their eyes. There is no addition beyond this number and no aspiration beyond it. Then He said: ﴿As a reward for what they used to do,﴾ thereby cutting off the hopes of those who wish. [[Mahmud said: "This is a cutting off of the hopes of those who wish." Ahmad said: He points to the People of the Sunnah, because they believe that the believer who disobeys is promised Paradise, and he must enter it in fulfilment of the true promise, and that no one deserves anything from God by his deeds. When he found His saying, exalted is He, ﴿As a reward for what they used to do﴾, he seized the opportunity to cite it in support of the doctrine of the Qadariyyah, that deeds are causes necessitating the reward. But there is no proof in that for their doctrine, given the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "None of you enters Paradise by his deed." It was said: "Not even you, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Not even I, unless God covers me with His grace and mercy." This hadith requires that the verse be interpreted in a way that reconciles it with the hadith. Either the verse is understood to mean the division of ranks among them in Paradise, which is according to their deeds, but this is not it, for what is mentioned in the verse is merely entry into Paradise, not the distribution of its degrees. Or, and this is the apparent meaning, God knows best, it is understood that when God promised the believer His Paradise—and His promise must be true and sincere, exalted and sanctified is He—the deeds became, by virtue of the promise, as though they were causes necessitating it, so they were treated in this expression as such. The purpose of that is to affirm the truthfulness of the promise in souls and to present it in the form of something merited by deeds, like a wage owed as a witness to the work, by way of figurative comparison, God knows best. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned the well-known hadith: "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has occurred to the heart of any man. Recite if you wish: 'No soul knows what is hidden for them of coolness of eyes.'" My grandfather, may God have mercy on him, used to prefer that the verse be recited after the mentioned hadith with the yā' of ukhfiya quiescent and referred to the first person, and it is among the widely transmitted readings. The reason for choosing that is to match the beginning of the hadith, which is: "I have prepared for My servants what no eye has seen nor ear heard," so that everything refers back to God, exalted is He, attributed explicitly to the pronoun of His name, and God is the Granter of success.]]: And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "God says: I have prepared for My righteous servants [[Agreed upon (by al-Bukhari and Muslim), through the chain of Abu al-Zinad from al-A'raj from Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him.]] what no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has occurred to the heart of any human being, let alone [[His saying "let alone what I have shown them of it." In al-Sihah, "bal" is a word built on fath like "kayf," and its meaning is "leave aside," as al-Akhfash permitted it in the verse of Ka'b ibn Malik: "He leaves the skulls, their crowns split open, let alone the hands, as though they had never been created." It is said its meaning is "other than." In the hadith: "I have prepared for My servants..." etc. (ʿ)]] what I have shown them of it. Recite if you wish: ﴿No soul knows what is hidden for them of coolness of eyes.﴾" And from al-Hasan, may God be pleased with him: the people concealed deeds in this world, so God concealed for them what no eye has seen nor ear has heard.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (*al-Kashshaf*) on surah 32, verses 18–21:

"Was a believer" and "was a defiant sinner" are construed according to the wording of *man* (whoever) in the verse ﴿Is one who was a believer like one who was a defiant sinner?﴾. "They are not equal" is construed according to its meaning. The evidence for this is His saying ﴿As for those who believed … and as for those who defied﴾, and similar to it His saying ﴿And among them are those who listen to you, until when they leave your presence﴾.

"The Gardens of Refuge" (*jannat al-ma'wa*) is a kind of garden. God says: ﴿And he had seen him another time, near the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, near which is the Garden of Refuge﴾. It was so named because of what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The spirits of the martyrs take refuge in it." It is also said that it is to the right of the Throne.

It was read as *jannat al-ma'wa* (singular "garden"), in the sense of unity.

﴿As a welcome, for what they used to do﴾. *Nuzul* (welcome, provision) is the gift offered to a guest, and then it became general.

﴿Then their refuge is the Fire﴾, that is, their place of safety and their dwelling. It is also permissible that the meaning is: "Then the Garden of their refuge is the Fire," that is, the Fire is for them in place of the Garden of Refuge that is for the believers.

Like His saying ﴿So give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾.

*Al-'adhab al-adna* (the nearer punishment) is the punishment of this world, such as killing and captivity, and what they were afflicted with of the famine [[His saying "and what they were afflicted with of the famine" means the famine that struck, or the meaning is drought, as is understood from *al-Sihah*. (Editor's note: ʿayn)]] of seven years. It is related from Mujahid, may Allah be pleased with him, that it is the punishment of the grave.

*Al-'adhab al-akbar* (the greater punishment) is the punishment of the Hereafter. That is: We make them taste the punishment of this world before they reach the Hereafter, ﴿so that perhaps they will return﴾, that is, repent from disbelief. Or the meaning is: "So that perhaps they will desire to return and seek it," like His saying ﴿Send us back, that we may do righteousness﴾. The desire to return has been called "returning," just as the desire to stand has been called "standing" in His saying ﴿When you rise to prayer﴾. This is supported by the reading of one who recited *yarji'un* (in the passive voice). [[Al-Zamakhshari said: "Its meaning is: perhaps they will repent. "They are not equal" is construed according to its meaning. The evidence for this is His saying ﴿As for those who believed … and as for those who defied﴾, and similar to it His saying ﴿And among them are those who listen to you, until when they leave your presence﴾.

"The Gardens of Refuge" (*jannat al-ma'wa*) is a kind of garden. God says: ﴿And he had seen him another time, near the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, near which is the Garden of Refuge﴾. It was so named because of what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The spirits of the martyrs take refuge in it." It is also said that it is to the right of the Throne.

It was read as *jannat al-ma'wa* (singular "garden"), in the sense of unity.

﴿As a welcome, for what they used to do﴾. *Nuzul* (welcome, provision) is the gift offered to a guest, and then it became general.

﴿Then their refuge is the Fire﴾, that is, their place of safety and their dwelling. It is also permissible that the meaning is: "Then the Garden of their refuge is the Fire," that is, the Fire is for them in place of the Garden of Refuge that is for the believers.

Like His saying ﴿So give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾.

*Al-'adhab al-adna* (the nearer punishment) is the punishment of this world, such as killing and captivity, and what they were afflicted with of the famine [[His saying "and what they were afflicted with of the famine" means the famine that struck, or the meaning is drought, as is understood from *al-Sihah*. That is: We make them taste the punishment of this world before they reach the Hereafter, ﴿so that perhaps they will return﴾, that is, repent from disbelief. Or the meaning is: "So that perhaps they will desire to return and seek it," like His saying ﴿Send us back, that we may do righteousness﴾. Then His saying ﴿thumma a'rada 'anha﴾ (then he turned away from them) is for expressing astonishment (istib'ad). The meaning is: turning away from the signs of God, given their clarity, their illumination, their guidance to the right path and their leading to the supreme happiness, after they have been reminded of them, is astonishing to reason and to justice. Just as you say to your companion: "I found such an opportunity, then you did not seize it," expressing astonishment at his failure to seize it. From this usage is the "thumma" (then) in the verse of the Hamasa:

لا يكشف الغمّاء إلا ابن حرّة ... يرى غمرات الموت ثمّ يزورها
Only the son of a noble mother removes the blinding calamity, one who sees the surges of death and then visits them.

نقاسمهم أسيافنا شر قسمة ... ففينا غواشيها وفيهم صدورها
We divide them with our swords in the worst division: the coverings of them are among us, and the breasts of them are among them.

It is by Ja'far ibn 'Ulba al-Harithi. He likened the blinding calamity (al-dahiya al-ghamma) to a perceptible thing that covers people and envelops them, by way of metaphor (al-makniyya), and "removing" (al-kashf) is an imaginative depiction (takhyil). He said "ibn hurra," i.e., noble, so as to stir the listener and urge him toward battle (al-hayja'). Al-ghamra: severity. Ghamarat al-mawt: its hardships and terrors, like the states of a fierce battle. His saying "thumma yazuruha" means he meets it willingly, like the meeting of a beloved, and its being joined with "thumma" is because between seeing the frightening terrors and descending into them willingly there is, customarily and rationally, a great distance. He likened the swords, extended and placed between them, to a thing in which division takes place, and "they divide us" is an imaginative depiction of that. Then he made it a consequence of that division that they have its coverings, i.e., what covers them of it, and these are its hilts (maqabidha). Or, because it exceeds the blade, it is a covering for him and for his enemies. "Sudurha" means its forward parts (atrafuha al-mutaqaddima), and the sadr (breast/front) of everything is its front. He expressed it with "fi" rather than "li," because "fi" conveys only the containment of the enemies by the breasts, as they enter their bodies, whereas "li" conveys ownership, which is not intended, though it would be implied by the division; perhaps he averted the suspicion of that by changing to "fi," and mentioning it first was a preparation for the second.

He finds it astonishing that someone would visit the surges of death after having seen them, become certain of them, and known their severity. If you say: why was it not said "innā minhu muntaqimūn" (indeed We will take vengeance from them)? I say: since He made him the greatest of all wrongdoers, then threatened the guilty generally with retribution from them, this indicates that the most wrongdoing one receives the largest share of retribution; had He said it with a pronoun, this benefit would not have been conveyed.

The Book (al-kitab) is generic, meaning the category of scripture, and the pronoun in liqa'ihi ("his encounter") refers back to it. The meaning is: We gave Musa (peace be upon him) the Book just as We gave you the Book, and he received revelation just as you received it. So do not be in doubt that you have received the like of what he received, or its equivalent. This is like His saying, ﴿So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you, ask those who read the Book before you﴾ (10:94). It is also like the phrase min liqa'ihi ("from his encounter") in His saying, ﴿And indeed, you receive the Qur'an from One who is All-Wise, All-Knowing﴾ (27:6), and His saying, ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection We will bring out for him a record which he will find laid open﴾ (17:13).

We made the Book revealed to Musa a guidance for his people, and We made from among them leaders (a'immah) who guide people and call them to what is in the Torah of God's religion and its laws, because of their patience and their certainty in the signs. Likewise, We will certainly make the Book revealed to you a guidance and a light, and We will certainly make from your community leaders who guide people with the same guidance, because of their steadfastness in supporting the religion and their firmness in certainty.

It has also been said: "from your encounter" means your encounter with Musa on the night of the Isra' (the Night Journey, the nocturnal journey of the Prophet), or on the Day of Resurrection. It has also been said: "from the encounter of Musa with the Book" means his receiving it with contentment and acceptance.

It is recited as lamma sabaru (لَمَّا صَبَرُوا) and as limasabaru (لِمَا صَبَرُوا), meaning "because of their patience." It is reported from al-Hasan (may God be pleased with him) that they were patient against this world.

It has also been said that God made the Torah a guidance for the Children of Israel specifically, and the descendants of Isma'il (peace be upon him) were not required to worship by what is in it. [The verse continues:] ﴿He will judge between them﴾, meaning He will decide, distinguishing the one who is right in his religion from the one who is false.

Zamakhshari's commentary (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 32, verse 26:

The wāw in "أَوَلَمْ يَهْدِ" (awa-lam yahdi, "Did it not guide...?") is a conjunction (ʿatf) coordinating with an implied antecedent of the same kind as what follows it. The pronoun in "لَهُمْ" (lahum, "for them") refers to the people of Makkah. It is recited with both the nūn and the yāʾ. The subject (fāʿil) is what is indicated by "كَمْ أَهْلَكْنا" (kam ahlaknā, "how many We destroyed"), because kam cannot function as a subject; one does not say "جاءني كم رجل" (jāʾanī kam rajulun, "how many a man came to me"). Its implied sense is: "Did it not guide them, the multitude of Our destroying the generations before them?"

Alternatively, this sentence stands as it is, with its own content and meaning, like your saying: "يعصم لا إله إلا الله الدماء والأموال" (yaʿṣimu lā ilāha illā Allāh al-dimāʾ wa-l-amwāl, "There is no god but Allah protects blood and property").

It is also permissible that the subject within it be a pronoun for God, as indicated by the recitation with the nūn.

"الْقُرُونِ" (al-qurūn, "the generations") refers to ʿĀd, Thamūd, and the people of Lūt.

"يَمْشُونَ فِي مَساكِنِهِمْ" (yamshūna fī masākinihim, "they walk in their dwellings") means the people of Makkah, who pass through their trading routes over the lands and abodes of those peoples.

It is also recited as "يمشون" (yamshūn) with the shadda (tashdīd), i.e., yumashshūn.

**Al-Kashshaf of al-Zamakhshari, commentary on Surah 32, verse 27:**

الْجُرُزِ: The land whose plants have been cut off (جرز), either because of lack of water, or because it was grazed and cleared. The word جرز is not used for land that does not grow plants, such as salt-flats (السباخ). Allah's words, "then We bring forth thereby crops," support this meaning. It is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that it is the land of Yemen. It is narrated from Mujahid, may Allah be pleased with him, that it is Abyan.

بِهِ: with the water. تَأْكُلُ: from the crops. أَنْعامُهُمْ: their livestock, from its fodder. وَأَنْفُسُهُمْ: and themselves, from its grain. It is also read as يَأْكُلُ, with the letter ya'.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 32, verses 28–30:**

Al-fath means victory, or judgment by decision, from His saying ﴿Our Lord, judge between us and our people in truth﴾. The Muslims used to say, "Allah will give us victory over the polytheists," and that He would decide between us and them. When the polytheists heard this, they said, ﴿When is this victory?﴾, that is, at what time will it happen, ﴿if you are truthful﴾ that it will occur. ﴿The Day of Victory﴾ is the Day of Resurrection, the day of separation between the believers and their enemies, and the day of their victory over them. It was said that it is the Day of Badr. It is also reported from Mujahid and al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it is the Day of the Conquest of Makkah.

If you ask: they asked about the time of the victory, so how does this statement fit as an answer to their question? I say: their purpose in asking about the time of the victory was to hasten it, in a manner of denial and mockery. So they were answered according to what was understood of their purpose in asking. It was said to them: ﴿Do not hasten it﴾ and do not mock. It is as if I see you on that day, when you have arrived there, and have believed, but belief did not benefit you, and you asked for respite in escaping the punishment, but you were not given respite.

If you ask: whoever interprets it as the Day of Conquest or the Day of Badr, how can it be right, according to his interpretation, that belief would not benefit them, when belief benefited the Tulaqa' (those freed after the conquest) on the Day of the Conquest of Makkah, and some people on the Day of Badr? I say: what is meant is that those among them who were killed, their belief will not benefit them at the moment of being killed, just as the belief of Pharaoh did not benefit him at the moment of drowning.

﴿So wait﴾ for the victory over them and their destruction. ﴿Indeed, they are waiting﴾ for your defeat and your destruction. This is like His saying, ﴿So wait, indeed We are with you among those who wait﴾.

Ibn al-Sumaiqa', may Allah have mercy on him, read ﴿munta⁠ẓirūn﴾ (they are waiting), with a fatha on the ẓā'.
